fixes.explanation: Jehoiakim was a king of Judah too, the son of Josiah (Jeremiah 36:1), so I see why he came to mind. But in this passage the LORD tells Jeremiah to go to Zedekiah king of Judah (Jeremiah 34:2). Same kingdom, different king. I once grabbed the dough for the sprinkle cookies and stamped the whole batch before I noticed it was the peppermint, so I know how easy it is to mix up two.

Ahab was a king of Israel (1 Kings 16:29), but he isn't the one in this passage. The LORD tells Jeremiah to speak to Zedekiah king of Judah (Jeremiah 34:2). Jerusalem is under attack, and Zedekiah is the king the message is for. Different king, different kingdom, friend. Everybody mixes up the kings sometimes.

Babylon it is. The LORD says to Zedekiah, “…you will go to Babylon.” (Jeremiah 34:3) He's captured, he meets the king of Babylon, and then he goes to the king's own country. That's a long trip, friend.

Egypt does show up in this chapter, but as the land the LORD brought Israel's forefathers out of, the house of slavery (Jeremiah 34:13). It isn't where Zedekiah is headed. The LORD says plainly that Zedekiah will go to Babylon (Jeremiah 34:3). Different spot on the map, friend.

Songs about victories aren't mentioned. The LORD says, “…people will burn spices for you and lament, ‘Alas, O master!’…” (Jeremiah 34:5) So it's burning spices and grieving. The verse compares the spices to those burned for the kings before him. It's a quiet honor, not a parade.

I get why plenty sounds right, but the text says the opposite. Babylon's army is fighting against Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah, including Lachish and Azekah. “For these were the only fortified cities remaining in Judah.” (Jeremiah 34:7) Two is not plenty.

That's what happens. The people agreed and released them, “…but later they changed their minds and took back the menservants and maidservants they had freed…” (Jeremiah 34:10-11) The text says they forced them to become slaves again. I think that one hurts, because the freedom ended only because the people changed their minds.

Third isn't the number the LORD gives. He says, “Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother…” and that he may serve six years before being let go (Jeremiah 34:14). The count is six years of service, and the seventh year is when he goes free. So the answer is seventh, friend.

The text names a different place. The LORD says they made the covenant “…before Me in the house that bears My Name.” (Jeremiah 34:15) That's the place He names, and a courtyard of the king isn't mentioned. The promise was made before Him in His house.

The text doesn't say that. The LORD says they were “…set at liberty to go wherever they wanted…” (Jeremiah 34:16) Working only for the king isn't part of it. The people later forced them back into slavery.
